meta.title: AI Lab Research Roadmap — Merged Master Plan
meta.author: @Arush
intro: This plan merges three sources into one sequence: your 21-paper "Break the Equation" curriculum (Modules 1–8), the [alisa-roadmap](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) GitHub knowledge map, and the blog it was compiled from, [Alisa Liu's Notes on the Industry Job Search](https://alisawuffles.github.io/blog/job-search/) (Research Scientist at OpenAI; 57 interviews, 11 companies, 4 offers). Her central finding sets the priority order here: technical skill and implementation fluency are evaluated far more than research experience, and research experience is mostly what gets you the first interview.
**The by-hand vs coding-agent rule.** Labs now expect you to use agents for real work, but interviews are run with AI off. So every item below carries one of three tags.

tags.meaning: Muscle memory. Write it from a blank file with AI off, under a time target, repeatedly.
tags.rule: Anything that fits in 15–60 lines and shows up in ML-coding rounds: attention, a decoder block, BPE, sampling, a training loop, NumPy backprop, Adam, LoRA, RoPE, a KV cache, the DPO/GRPO loss.

tags.meaning: Write the core once by hand so you own it, then hand the variations, sweeps, plots and scaffolding to a coding agent.
tags.rule: The "break it" experiments: you write the 10-line change that breaks the equation; the agent builds the harness, dataset loader, logging and plots around it.

tags.meaning: Delegate the build; your job is to specify it, read every line, run it, and be able to explain any design choice in it.
tags.rule: Triton kernels, distributed training scaffolding, full RLHF loops with TRL, MoE training infra, diffusion samplers, anything that is in a project on your CV but would never be asked as a 30-minute whiteboard.

afterTags: The test for a CV project is simple: if an interviewer opens any file in it and asks "why is this here?", you answer without hesitation. Being able to reproduce the whole file by hand is not required; being able to reproduce the boilerplate core (the model, the loss, the loop) is.

**Reading order.** Phases run roughly in sequence but overlap on purpose: LeetCode (Phase 5) is a daily 30-minute habit from week 3 onward, and the paper curriculum (Phase 3) is the spine that the CS336 lectures and the muscle-memory drills hang off. Every section links its sources inline; the full index is at the end.

interviews.title: What AI-lab interviews actually test
interviews.intro: ML coding is the single most common round, and "implement a Transformer / decoding strategy / classic ML algorithm from scratch in PyTorch" is its modal question. Everything else in this roadmap is weighted by the table below, which is Alisa's own breakdown (approximate shares from the GitHub map).

rounds.testing: Can you implement what you claim to know, fluently, with AI off? PyTorch is a must; NumPy only for backward passes.
rounds.passing: Decoder block with causal masking from a blank file; beam search or top-p sampling clean on first run.

rounds.testing: Two flavors: (a) design an experiment to answer a research question and defend it under pushback; (b) rapid-fire breadth ("What is 5D parallelism? PPO vs GRPO? Ways to encode position?").
rounds.passing: Crisp, opinionated answers; you can name trade-offs without notes.

rounds.testing: LeetCode-style, sometimes with ML flavor; the patterns leak into ML coding rounds.
Specific stories mapped to leadership / conflict / failure / impact, plus a serious question on AI safety.
rounds.passing: STAR answers retrieved instantly, no reconstruction.

rounds.testing: Pen-and-paper derivations: MLE = cross-entropy, KL both directions, backprop, Adam bias correction, SVD/low-rank.
Why you chose the problems you did; what you'd do with 10x compute; the company's recent papers.
rounds.passing: 80% of the talk on first-author work; every baseline choice defensible.

interviews.after: Two practical notes from the blog that shape the schedule: each interview is "a class you never attended with three days to cram," so keep swappable per-topic notes (she kept a [running LLM notebook](https://alisawuffles.notion.site/alisa-s-book-of-llms) and a [math notebook](https://alisawuffles.notion.site/math-notes)); and sleep beats last-minute cramming — her first technical interview was lost to an off-by-one error on two hours of sleep.

phases.title: Breadth first — Stanford CS336
intro: Watch all 17 lectures of [Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch](https://cs336.stanford.edu/spring2025/) ([YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLoROMvodv4rOY23Y0BoGoBGgQ1zmU_MT_)) before any deep dive. Alisa started her search this way; it gives the skeleton that organizes every scattered concept, and its five assignments are the best self-study implementation track that exists. Watch at 1.5x, take notes, draw one diagram per lecture. Do not pause to implement yet.

playlist.title: Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

lectures.why: BPE appears in almost every ML-coding round
Memory math (params, activations, KV) comes up constantly
Backbone of every architecture question: pre-norm, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE
"Train a 70B model on 8x80GB — walk me through it"
Same question, deeper: ZeRO stages, TP/PP/DP trade-offs
KV cache size formula, speculative decoding, PagedAttention
IsoFLOP curves, parametric loss fits, LR schedule pitfalls
"How would you know your model got better?"
Curation and dedup are underrated and commonly asked
PPO vs GRPO is a standard rapid-fire question

after: **Assignment plan.** [A1 Basics](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment1-basics) is HAND: tokenizer, model, optimizer, training loop, written with autocomplete off (the course itself asks for this). Alisa calls it crucial because implementing and debugging a Transformer comes up so often that it must become muscle memory. A2, A3, A4, A5 are HAND→AGENT: write the core (the online-softmax tile, the IsoFLOP fit, the dedup pass, the GRPO loss) yourself, let agents build the harnesses. Compute for self-study: a single H100 runs ~$2–3/hour on [RunPod](https://runpod.io/pricing) or [Lambda](https://lambda.ai/pricing); debug on CPU first.

phases.title: Math foundations
intro: At least one company will run a dedicated math interview, from logic puzzles to pen-and-paper derivations. Everything here is HAND: derive on paper, then confirm numerically in a 10-line script. Each derivation is paired with the paper in Phase 3 that uses it, so the math is never studied in isolation.

rows.derive: Bernoulli → Binomial → Gaussian limit; 68-95-99.7; CLT; multivariate Gaussian
rows.code: Sample 10k Bernoullis, plot the binomial mean converging to a Gaussian

rows.derive: MLE: show minimizing cross-entropy is maximizing log-likelihood
rows.code: Train logistic regression with both losses, assert identical gradients

rows.derive: MAP: show L2 regularization equals a Gaussian prior
Entropy; derive perplexity = exp(H); cross-entropy vs KL
rows.code: Compute PPL of a tiny LM two ways

rows.derive: KL(P ‖ Q) vs KL(Q ‖ P): mode-seeking vs mass-covering; which direction the RLHF penalty uses and why
rows.code: Fit a 1-Gaussian to a 2-Gaussian mixture under each direction, plot

rows.derive: Matmul FLOPs: (m×k)@(k×n) = 2mnk; derive 6ND for Transformer training
rows.code: Count FLOPs for a 124M GPT-2 by hand, check with `torch.utils.flop_counter`

rows.derive: SVD $A = U \Sigma V^\top$; Eckart–Young: rank-r truncation minimizes Frobenius error
rows.code: SVD a fine-tuned ΔW, plot singular values, verify most mass is in top-r

rows.derive: Eigendecomposition of symmetric matrices; matrix norms (L1, L2, Frobenius, nuclear) and what each regularizes
Chain rule for a 2-layer MLP; Jacobians for vector→vector maps
rows.code: NumPy forward+backward for linear → softmax → cross-entropy, no autograd; assert against `torch.autograd`

rows.derive: Adam update rule; why m̂ and v̂ need bias correction at step 1
rows.code: Your 25-line Adam from Module 1, with and without correction

rows.derive: Policy gradient: the log-derivative trick, reward-to-go, why a state-only baseline is unbiased
rows.code: REINFORCE on a 3-armed bandit, with and without baseline, plot variance

after: **Study order.** Read [CS231n backprop notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/) first (the NumPy backward pass is asked verbatim). Then Hamish Ivison's [Introduction to Policy Gradient for LMs](https://ivison.id.au/2026/02/09/policy-gradient.html), which derives REINFORCE → baselines → importance weighting → group-relative advantages in LM notation; read it before touching PPO or GRPO. Supplement with Lilian Weng's [Policy Gradient Algorithms](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2018-04-08-policy-gradient/) and Chip Huyen's [ML Interviews Book](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/) to find gaps.
phases.sources: [alisa-roadmap README, Phase 2](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [Notes on the Industry Job Search](https://alisawuffles.github.io/blog/job-search/)

phases.title: Muscle-memory implementations
intro: This is the HAND list: the boilerplate core you must reproduce from a blank file, with every AI tool off, under the time target. Alisa's rule, which the CS336 honor code also enforces: practice with AI assistance completely off, because you will underestimate your reliance otherwise. Rotate through the table once a week until every row is under target three times in a row; after that, one timed row per day keeps it warm.

drills.name: Scaled dot-product attention
drills.must: The √d_k scaling, −∞ (not 0) in the causal mask, softmax over the key axis

drills.name: Multi-head attention
drills.must: Split heads → attend → merge via reshape or `einsum`; output projection W_O

drills.name: Full pre-norm decoder block
drills.must: LN → MHA → residual → LN → FFN (4×d_model, GeLU or SwiGLU) → residual; parameter count by hand

drills.name: BPE tokenizer
drills.must: Build vocab from a corpus; encode a new string; state the merge-step complexity

drills.name: Top-k / top-p sampling with temperature
drills.must: Temperature before filtering; masking that keeps at least one token

drills.name: Beam search
drills.must: Track log-probs across B beams; handle EOS and length normalization

drills.name: Full training loop
drills.must: Forward, loss, `backward()`, optimizer step, scheduler step, grad clipping, eval split

drills.name: NumPy backprop
drills.must: Linear → softmax → cross-entropy, analytic gradients, no autograd

drills.name: Adam optimizer
drills.must: m, v, bias correction, decoupled weight decay

drills.name: LoRA wrapper around `nn.Linear`
drills.must: B = 0 init, A ~ N(0, σ²), α/r scaling, merge for inference

drills.name: RoPE
drills.must: Complex rotation of Q and K; dot product depends only on m − n

drills.name: KV cache for generation
drills.must: Prefill vs decode; append K, V per step; compute only the new Q

drills.name: GQA / MQA attention
drills.must: n_kv_heads < n_heads via `repeat_interleave`; KV-cache memory drops by n_heads/n_kv_heads

drills.name: GRPO advantage + clipped loss
drills.must: Group-normalized advantages, importance ratio with stop-gradient on old log-probs, clip

drills.name: PPO clipped surrogate + GAE
drills.must: `min(rA, clip(r,1−ε,1+ε)A)`, GAE recursion, value loss, entropy bonus

drills.name: Online (tiled) softmax
drills.must: Running max and denominator rescaled by exp(m_old − m_new); `allclose` vs `F.softmax`

drills.name: Top-k MoE router
drills.must: Softmax gate, top-2 dispatch, load-balancing auxiliary loss

drills.name: Flow-matching loss + Euler sampler
drills.must: x_t = (1−t)x₀ + t x₁, v_θ ≈ x₁ − x₀, Euler loop

playlist.title: Karpathy — Neural Networks: Zero to Hero

after: **Reference implementations to read once, then close.** Karpathy's [build-nanogpt](https://github.com/karpathy/build-nanogpt) and [minbpe](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe) ([Neural Networks: Zero to Hero playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAqhIrjkxbuWI23v9cThsA9GvCAUhRvKZ)), [The Illustrated GPT-2](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-gpt2/), and the [CS224N self-attention and Transformers notes](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/readings/cs224n-self-attention-transformers-2023_draft.pdf). Read them before the first drill, never during one.

**AGENT work around the drills.** Have a coding agent build you a drill harness: a repo with one `test_<row>.py` per row that asserts your from-scratch output against the PyTorch reference, plus a timer. You write the implementation files; the agent writes and maintains the tests.
phases.sources: [alisa-roadmap README, Phase 3](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [Notes on the Industry Job Search](https://alisawuffles.github.io/blog/job-search/)

phases.title: The 21-paper curriculum, merged with the concept deep-dives
intro: Your paper sequence stays intact; what changes is that each paper now also carries the interview questions and "what to master" items from Alisa's map, and each experiment carries a HAND / HAND→AGENT / AGENT tag. The weekly loop per paper (Day 1 read, Day 2 derive and watch, Day 3 break it) is in the Execution section. Paper 1 (AlexNet) is already done in your notebook; start at Paper 2.
after: **What goes on the CV from this phase.** Two or three of the HAND→AGENT experiments, polished into small public repos with a README that states the hypothesis, the one-line change that broke the equation, and the plot. Candidates: the Transformer scaling/masking ablation (#4), the MoE routing-collapse study (#18), and the GRPO group-size study (#19). These are the ones you can defend line by line in a technical discussion.
phases.sources: your 21-paper roadmap PDF · [alisa-roadmap README, Phase 1](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [Ivison, Introduction to Policy Gradient for LMs](https://ivison.id.au/2026/02/09/policy-gradient.html) · [Manohar, Lightweight Guide to GRPO](https://gitlostmurali.com/blog/grpo-intro)

phases.title: Systems and infra topics the papers skip
intro: Five topic clusters from Alisa's map have no paper in your curriculum but appear constantly in rapid-fire technical discussions. Each gets a reading, a small HAND implementation, and the specific question it is known to unlock.

clusters.name: Tokenization
clusters.master: BPE merge algorithm; WordPiece vs SentencePiece; pre-tokenization and Unicode normalization; why " hello" and "hello" differ; vocab-size trade-off (fewer tokens per sentence vs more embedding params); why bad tokenization hurts code and multilingual models
clusters.question: "Time complexity of the merge step?" "Why does tokenizer efficiency shift the Chinchilla frontier?"

clusters.name: Inference and the KV cache
clusters.master: Prefill (parallel) vs decode (sequential); KV cache size = 2 × n_layers × seq_len × d_model × bytes; what happens when VRAM runs out; speculative decoding (~2–3x); PagedAttention as OS-style virtual memory; greedy vs beam vs top-k vs top-p vs temperature and the failure modes of each
clusters.hand: KV cache for generation, 20 min; top-k/top-p and beam search (Phase 2)
clusters.question: "70B model, 96 layers, d_model 8192, bf16, one 128K sequence — how much KV memory?" (~200 GB)

clusters.name: Distributed training
clusters.master: Data parallel (AllReduce gradients) vs tensor parallel (split weight matrices, AllGather activations) vs pipeline parallel (micro-batches to shrink the bubble) vs expert parallel; ZeRO stages 1–3; rematerialization, gradient accumulation, host offload; roofline reasoning (compute vs memory vs communication bound); "5D parallelism"
clusters.hand: A memory-math worksheet: params, grads, Adam states, activations per GPU under each scheme (HAND, on paper); the distributed trainer itself is AGENT, from CS336 A2
clusters.question: "8 × 80 GB A100s, 70B model — walk me through memory math and parallelism strategy." "What is 5D parallelism?"

clusters.name: Evaluation
clusters.master: Perplexity vs downstream benchmarks; contamination; pass@k; LM-as-judge pitfalls; why a benchmark gain can be a metric artifact (ties into the emergence debate)
clusters.hand: A pass@k estimator from n samples (10 lines)
clusters.question: "How would you know if your model got better?"

clusters.name: Data
clusters.master: Common Crawl → usable text: language ID, quality filters, exact and fuzzy dedup (MinHash), PII removal; data mixing and curriculum
clusters.hand: MinHash dedup on a small corpus (HAND→AGENT)
clusters.question: "Design a filtering pipeline and tell me how you'd validate it."

after: **The scaling book.** [How to Scale Your Model](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/) (Austin et al., Google DeepMind) is the reference for the infra cluster. Read chapters 1, 4, 5 and 7 in full and work the exercises; skim 2, 3 and 12 for notation; chapters 6 and 8 (training and serving Llama 3) are the worked examples to reproduce the arithmetic for on paper.
phases.sources: [alisa-roadmap README, Phase 1 and 2 sections](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [CS336 Spring 2025](https://cs336.stanford.edu/spring2025/) · [How to Scale Your Model](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

phases.title: General coding fluency
intro: Target: LeetCode Mediums consistently under 25 minutes, with AI off. This is a daily habit, not a phase, because algorithmic patterns leak into ML-coding rounds (top-K heaps are decoding; sliding windows are sliding-window attention; DP is beam search and edit distance). Alisa's two lists are the whole syllabus: [LeetCode 75](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/leetcode-75/) first, then [NeetCode Blind 75](https://neetcode.io/practice/practice/blind75).

topics.reach: Including search on the answer space
DFS, BFS, LCA; trees disguised as graphs
1D and 2D; memo vs tabulation; edit distance, coin change, LCS
Quick, merge, heap; time and space for each

after: Keep a one-line log per problem (pattern, time, mistake). Every two weeks, redo the five slowest.
phases.sources: [alisa-roadmap README, Phase 4](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [Notes on the Industry Job Search, Appendix](https://alisawuffles.github.io/blog/job-search/)

phases.title: Research portfolio, technical discussion, job talk, behavioral
intro: Research gets you the interview; this phase makes sure you can defend it. Alisa's framing: the technical-discussion round is the most underrated, and the behavioral round is the one she failed first by assuming she was "obviously well-behaved" and then going blank.

**Build the portfolio (AGENT-heavy, HAND-defensible).** As a student without a PhD paper trail, your CV projects are the research record. Aim for three public projects by week 20, each with a hypothesis, an ablation, a plot, and a README written in the "why I did it" voice:

portfolio.text: One from the Phase 3 break-it experiments (see the CV note at the end of Phase 3).

One systems project: a from-scratch GPT-2 124M reproduction on [build-nanogpt](https://github.com/karpathy/build-nanogpt) with your own throughput log, or [CS336 A2](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment2-systems)'s FlashAttention-2 Triton kernel with a benchmark table.
One post-training project: the mini-GRPO or DPO run from [CS336 A5](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment5-alignment), with reward curves and a failure-mode study (β = 0, G = 2).

phases.afterPortfolio: For each, the HAND core (model, loss, loop) is yours; the harness, sweeps and plots are the agent's; and you must be able to answer "why is this line here?" for every file. Write the design-choice list before you consider a project done.

prep.title: Technical and research discussion prep
prep.text: For every project, write a one-page "why" narrative, not a "what" summary: every major design choice with its defensible reason, what you tried that failed, what you would do differently, and what you would do with 10x the compute. Form opinions on three to five research directions you believe in right now. Tailor the pitch to the role: interviewers are tired, so hit the keywords of the team's area.

prep.title: Rapid-fire set, out loud
prep.text: Drill the rapid-fire set out loud, with AI as the examiner: ways to encode position; 5D parallelism; PPO vs GRPO; pre- vs post-norm; LoRA layer choice; why Flash Attention is faster without changing the math; the KV-cache formula; Chinchilla's N* and D*. Read the target company's last six months of papers and reference them naturally.

prep.title: Job talk (if asked)
prep.text: 45–60 minutes, 80%+ on first-author or lead-author work, second-author and ongoing work in the last 10 minutes. Expect deep Q&A on every baseline and experimental choice; rehearse with people who push back hard.

prep.title: Behavioral
prep.text: Write down five to ten memorable stories now and map each to leadership, conflict, failure, impact, collaboration in STAR form, so retrieval is instant. Prepare specific answers to "Why this company?" and to "What is your view on AI safety and responsible development?" — frontier labs ask the second one seriously and want a considered position. After every interview, record notes the same day; they feed the next cram.

phases.sources: [alisa-roadmap README, Phases 5–7](https://github.com/soasme/alisa-roadmap) · [Notes on the Industry Job Search](https://alisawuffles.github.io/blog/job-search/)

phases.title: Getting in the door — networking, sequencing, negotiation
intro: One referral is worth roughly forty cold applications (cold applications reply at ~1–2%, referrals at ~20%+), so the pipeline is built months before you need it, in parallel with everything above.

items.text: Be visible at NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, EMNLP — talk to people, don't just attend. Workshops and poster sessions are easier entry points for a student.
Collaborate across institutions; co-authors become referrers. Open-source contributions to repos labs actually use (vLLM, TRL, nanoGPT forks, CS336 leaderboards) are the student equivalent.
Reach out informally months before searching: nobody refers a stranger. Reconnecting with people you haven't spoken to in years is normal and expected.
Ask advisors, classmates and collaborators who already moved to industry. Use friends and recruiters to learn which teams actually have headcount; that can matter more than your preparation.
Apply to less-desired companies first; they are practice, not consolation prizes. Watch your stamina — do not burn out before the companies you care about.
Do not open your top-choice processes until you hold at least one offer; leverage multiplies.
Time processes so offers land close together. Deadlines are flexible and recruiters expect you to finish other processes, but investigate each company's reputation for "exploding" offers.
Customize prep per company: recent papers, research agenda, product. Each interview is a slightly different class with three days to cram, so keep per-topic notes you can swap in.

after: **Negotiate.** The work is not done at the offer. Initial offers leave room by design and recruiters will say so. Before every recruiter call, write down what you will and will not share and a few lines you can say verbatim; anticipate their questions. Lean on friends for market data points. A few weeks of effort here can equal years of pay difference at the initial number.

papers.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.approach: Sections 3–4: non-saturating ReLU (6x faster than tanh), overlapping pooling, PCA color augmentation, dropout p=0.5.
papers.hooks: "Why did depth + GPUs + regularization unlock representation learning?"

experiments.body: Swap ReLU for tanh/sigmoid in a 5-layer CIFAR-10 CNN, plot per-layer `param.grad.norm()`.
Remove dropout and weight decay, watch train acc hit 100% while val loss explodes.

papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
papers.approach: Algorithm 1 and Section 3 (bias correction). How $m_t$ (momentum) and $v_t$ (uncentered variance) combine AdaGrad and RMSProp.
papers.hooks: (math round): derive the update, explain why bias correction matters at step 1.

experiments.body: 25-line custom `torch.optim.Optimizer`; delete the $/(1-\beta_1^t)$ and $/(1-\beta_2^t)$ divisions and watch the first steps jump because $v_1 \approx 0$.
Sweep L2-in-gradient vs decoupled AdamW across LRs.

papers.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
papers.approach: Separate vanishing gradients (fixed by BatchNorm) from the degradation problem (deeper plain nets have higher training error). Why $F(x) = H(x) - x$ is easier than learning identity.
papers.hooks: "What training failure do residuals prevent?" (asked in the Transformer section too).

experiments.body: `out = block(x) + alpha * x` with alpha ∈ {0, 1}, 20- vs 56-layer on CIFAR-10; watch the 56-layer plain net lose.
Zero-init the last BatchNorm γ in each block so blocks start as identity (the same trick reappears in #20 DiT).

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.approach: Section 3.2 and Table 1. Why $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ stops variance growing with $d_k$; $O(1)$ max path length.
papers.hooks: **Must master (rapid-fire):** parameter count for d_model=1024, 16 heads, 24 layers, 50K vocab; why FFN expands to 4×d_model; pre-norm vs post-norm gradient flow; LayerNorm vs RMSNorm; ReLU → GeLU → SwiGLU; why modern models drop dropout; what individual heads learn; sinusoidal vs learned vs RoPE vs ALiBi ([RoPE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864), [ALiBi paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409)) and why absolute encodings fail past training length.

experiments.body: Remove `/ math.sqrt(d_k)` at d_k=512, feed random normal Q, K, inspect `Q.grad` — softmax goes one-hot and gradients vanish.
Change −inf to 0 in the causal mask; val loss collapses to ~0 while generation is garbage.

papers.note: This is the single most-asked implementation; the full decoder block is Phase 2 row 3.

papers.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words
papers.approach: How 16×16 patching removes CNN inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance). Figure 7: RGB PCA filters, position-embedding cosine similarity, attention distance by depth. Takeaway: scale beats inductive bias past ~14M images.

experiments.body: Tiny ViT vs ResNet-18 on 5k CIFAR-10 images; ResNet wins.
Zero `pos_embedding`, shuffle patches, verify the [CLS] output is identical (permutation equivariance).

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.approach: Figure 1.2 and Section 3: in-context learning with no weight updates; scaling curves on WordScramble and translation. Read the data section (Common Crawl filtering, dedup) alongside CS336 Data lectures.

experiments.body: Follow build-nanogpt and log tokens/sec as you enable `set_float32_matmul_precision('high')`, bf16 autocast, `torch.compile`, FlashAttention, and vocab padding 50257 → 50304.
Few-shot label-flipping (Great movie → Negative) on an open 7B model to see scale override priors.

papers.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.approach: The deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy). Why experience replay breaks temporal correlation and why a target network stabilizes moving Bellman targets.

experiments.body: 100-line DQN on `CartPole-v1`; set replay buffer = batch_size, or update the target net every step — Q-values diverge.
Frame-stacking ablation.

papers.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

resources.label: Ivison: Policy Gradient for LMs (read first)

papers.approach: Trace why vanilla PG collapses when one step moves the policy too far. Equation 7 (clipped surrogate) and GAE. First-order clipping buys TRPO-style trust-region stability cheaply.
papers.hooks: **Rapid-fire:** PPO vs GRPO — PPO keeps a learned value/critic, GRPO replaces it with group-normalized rewards.

experiments.body: In CleanRL's `ppo.py` on LunarLander, delete `torch.clamp(ratio, 1−ε, 1+ε)` and raise `update_epochs` 4 → 20; KL spikes, policy collapses to one action.
Disable advantage normalization and watch variance explode.

papers.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
papers.approach: Derive the closed-form forward jump $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$. Section 3.2: why predicting $\epsilon$ with MSE equals the ELBO and score matching.

experiments.body: Tiny DDPM on MNIST; switch the U-Net target from $\epsilon$ to $x_0$ and see blurry samples (Table 2).
Set the Langevin noise $z = 0$ at every reverse step and watch deterministic sampling fail under the DDPM formulation.

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.approach: Intrinsic rank (Li et al. 2018). Section 4: freeze $W_0$, inject $\Delta W = (\alpha/r)BA$, $B = 0$ and $A \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$; Tables 5–6: adapting $W_q$ and $W_v$ at r=4 beats $W_q$ alone at r=64.
papers.hooks: **Rapid-fire:** which layers to adapt (q, v vs all linear); when LoRA loses to full fine-tuning; [QLoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) (NF4 base + bf16 adapters, double quantization); adapters, prefix tuning, IA³. SVD from Phase 1 is the math.

experiments.body: 15-line `nn.Linear` wrapper. Init both A and B to zero (gradients identically zero, a saddle) or both Gaussian (ΔW ≠ 0 at step 0, corrupting the base).
Rank sweep r ∈ {1, 4, 64}; plot singular values of ΔW.

papers.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
papers.approach: The SFT → reward model → PPO-ptx pipeline. Bradley–Terry loss $-\log\sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l))$; the per-token KL penalty $\beta \log(\pi_{RL}/\pi_{SFT})$ as the anti-reward-hacking term.
papers.hooks: **Rapid-fire:** why SFT masks loss on prompt tokens; a 1.3B aligned model is preferred over 175B unaligned.

experiments.body: Build the toy RLHF loop (GPT-2 policy, DistilBERT sentiment reward, TRL).
Set β = 0 and watch the policy degenerate into "excellent! best! 10/10!" — Goodhart's law live.

papers.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
papers.approach: [Kaplan et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) vs Hoffmann: three IsoFLOP methods, $L(N, D) = E + A/N^\alpha + B/D^\beta$, FLOPs ≈ 6ND, ~20 tokens/parameter.
papers.hooks: The equation every candidate must know cold: $N^* \propto C^{0.5}$, $D^* \propto C^{0.5}$. Also: why tokenizer efficiency shifts the frontier; the emergent-abilities debate (real phase transitions vs metric artifacts).

experiments.body: NumPy script for $L(N, D) = 1.69 + 406.4/N^{0.34} + 410.7/D^{0.28}$ under $C = 6ND$; plot loss vs N per FLOP budget.
Train a tiny Transformer 2,000 steps with `CosineAnnealingLR(T_max=10000)` vs `T_max=2000` and see why Kaplan was fooled by not decaying to zero.

papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
papers.approach: Derive Section 4 on paper: solve the KL-constrained reward maximization for $r(x, y) = \beta \log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{ref}) + \beta \log Z(x)$, plug into Bradley–Terry, watch $Z(x)$ cancel. Any LM is implicitly a reward model; RLHF becomes stable binary cross-entropy with no critic and no online sampling.

experiments.body: The 6-line loss (Phase 2 row 14).
Remove `ref_logps` (naive unlikelihood training) or set β = 0.001 vs 5.0; probability mass collapses onto degenerate tokens.

papers.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
papers.approach: Continuous SSM → zero-order-hold discretization → why LTI models (S4) fail selective copying and induction heads. Input-dependent $B, C, \Delta$ break the convolution, requiring a parallel associative scan (Blelloch 1990). $O(N)$ with Transformer-quality modeling.

experiments.body: Synthetic selective-copying dataset; static LTI recurrence vs selective ($B_t = W_B x_t$); LTI fails to filter variable-spaced noise.
Blelloch prefix-sum scan in PyTorch, $O(N)$ sequential → $O(\log N)$ parallel.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

videos.title: Stanford CS25: Jason Wei on CoT

papers.approach: Why few-shot prompting has a flat scaling curve on GSM8K. CoT as adaptive test-time compute via an externalized scratchpad (Nye et al. 2021). Emergent at scale when intermediate states are materialized as tokens.

experiments.body: Harness that force-decodes a wrong intermediate step ("14 × 3 = 99") on GSM8K and measures whether the model self-corrects.
Self-consistency, K=10 samples at T=0.7 with majority vote; expect +10–15% over greedy.

papers.title: LLaMA (2023) and Llama 3 (2024)
papers.approach: Contrast every block with #4: pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE (relative position via 2D complex rotation), GQA. Inference-optimal models over-train small architectures on 15T+ tokens and shrink the KV cache via GQA.
papers.hooks: **Rapid-fire:** KV cache size = 2 × n_layers × seq_len × d_model × bytes (a 70B model at 128K tokens in bf16 needs ~200 GB); GQA reduces it by n_heads/n_kv_heads.

experiments.body: RoPE in 15 lines via `torch.polar`; verify $\langle \mathrm{RoPE}(q, m), \mathrm{RoPE}(k, n) \rangle$ depends only on $m - n$; then exceed `max_seq_len` without frequency scaling.
Profile VRAM with $H_{kv} = 32$ vs 4.

papers.title: FlashAttention (2022) and FlashAttention-2 (2023)
papers.approach: Memory-bound vs compute-bound (arithmetic intensity). Standard attention writes an $O(N^2)$ matrix to HBM; Section 3's tiling and online softmax (running max $m$, running sum $\ell$) keep it exact and in SRAM.
papers.hooks: **Rapid-fire:** "Flash Attention doesn't change the math, so why is it 5–10x faster?"

experiments.body: Tiled online softmax over a 10,000-vector in chunks of 100, `allclose` vs `F.softmax`.
Naive `Q @ K.T` at N=16,384 (CUDA OOM) vs `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`.
The Triton FlashAttention-2 kernel from CS336 A2 — you must be able to explain every tile boundary, not write it blind.

papers.title: Switch Transformers (2021) and DeepSeek-V3 (2024)
papers.approach: Replacing the dense FFN with E experts + a top-k router decouples parameters (capacity) from FLOPs per token. Routing collapse and its fixes: load-balancing auxiliary loss vs DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free bias adjustment. Conditional compute is how 600B+ models serve fast.

experiments.body: Mini MoE with 8 experts and a top-2 softmax router, no balancing loss; histogram of expert utilization over 500 steps shows 1–2 experts taking >95% and the rest dying.
Add the aux loss, then the bias trick, re-plot.

papers.title: DeepSeekMath (2024, GRPO) and DeepSeek-R1 (2025)

videos.title: Coding GRPO From Scratch in PyTorch

resources.label: Murali's Lightweight Guide to GRPO (no RL prerequisite)
Ivison's policy-gradient notes (goes as far as CISPO)

papers.approach: Connect #8 PPO + #15 CoT. GRPO drops the critic: sample G completions per prompt, $\hat{A}_i = (r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r))/\mathrm{std}(r)$, importance ratio with stop-gradient on old log-probs, clip at ε.
papers.hooks: Know the neighbors: RLOO (leave-one-out), REINFORCE++, VinePPO, CISPO; why most 2025 implementations set the KL coefficient β = 0 (clipping already bounds the step); on- vs off-policy trade-off; the "forking tokens" result.

experiments.body: Build the mini-GRPO loop (TRL or Unsloth) on Qwen2.5-1.5B with GSM8K or Countdown and a rule-based reward (+1 format, +2 correct).
The loss itself (Phase 2 row 15).
G = 8 → 2, advantages become too noisy; plot `<think>` length growing over steps.

papers.title: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers
papers.approach: #5 ViT + #9 DDPM. Patchify latents into tokens; adaLN-Zero injects t and class c by predicting $(\gamma, \beta, \alpha)$ with the final linear layer zero-initialized so each block starts as identity. More GFLOPs → lower FID.

experiments.body: One DiT block with the conditioning MLP; zero-init its final linear vs Xavier and watch early convergence speed (the ResNet zero-γ trick again).
The full latent-diffusion training scaffold.

papers.title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
papers.approach: Contrast with #9. Straight-line interpolation $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$, train $v_\theta(x_t, t) \approx x_1 - x_0$, sample with an ODE solver. Straight optimal-transport paths give good samples in 10–20 Euler steps instead of 1,000.

experiments.body: 50-line 2D flow matching on Two Moons / Swiss Roll, 3-layer MLP, Euler loop with N=5 steps vs DDPM at N=5; plot trajectories.

execution.intro: Each paper takes three days; the remaining two weekdays go to CS336 assignments and the portfolio. This keeps your original Day 1–3 loop and adds Alisa's two habits: explain it aloud, and keep running notes.

steps.title: Read and question
steps.body: Read the paper's methodology, equations and ablation tables, not the intro. Write three questions you cannot yet answer.

steps.title: Derive and watch
steps.body: Watch the paired walkthrough, then write the core derivation by hand (the √d_k variance argument, the DPO cancellation, the GRPO advantage). Add the result to your running LLM notebook.

steps.title: Break it
steps.body: Run the experiment: you write the one change that breaks the equation; a coding agent builds the harness, data loader and plots. Save the plot and a two-line conclusion.

steps.title: Explain it aloud
steps.body: Ten minutes with an LLM as examiner, no notes. If you cannot explain it simply, you do not know it yet; repeat Day 2.

steps.title: Drills and review
steps.body: One full timed drill rotation from Phase 2 (AI off) and the week's LeetCode review.
